title: Making Cured Bacon at Home (PNW 784, August 2025)
org: Oregon State University Extension Service (Pacific Northwest Extension; J. Waite-Cusic, J. Hibbard-Swanson)
licence_note: Copyright Oregon State University. Read by R12 on 2026-11-16: Curing Salt #1 is 6.25% sodium nitrite and 93.75% salt; recipes use 1 teaspoon Curing Salt #1 per 5 lb pork belly; cure in a refrigerator at 40 F; cook to 160 F; nitrite and nitrate salts have relatively high toxicity and are used only in researched quantities; nitrate blends (Prague Powder #2) not recommended for bacon.

title: 9 CFR 424.21, Use of food ingredients and sources of radiation (curing agents table: sodium or potassium nitrite)
org: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (Code of Federal Regulations, Title 9)
licence_note: US federal regulation, public domain. Read by R12 on 2026-11-16 (govinfo CFR 2024 edition): sodium or potassium nitrite, 1 oz to 100 lb meat (dry cure); 1/4 oz to 100 lb chopped meat; not more than 200 ppm nitrite in finished product; bacon per paragraph (b), 120 ppm ingoing; nitrites not in baby, junior or toddler foods.

title: Toxicological Profile for Nitrate and Nitrite (July 2017)

title: Storing Canned Goods (B. Nummer, B. Jahner)
licence_note: Copyright Utah State University. Read by R12 on 2026-11-16: canned food remains safe as long as the seal is not broken; do not let cans or jars freeze (bursting, broken seals); discard badly dented, bulging, rusty or leaky cans; commercial code date usually 2-5 years from manufacture; high-acid foods have a shorter shelf life; home canned: one year, use before two years.

title: Prairie Fare: Is It Time for an Oil Change in Your Kitchen? (J. Garden-Robinson, April 20, 2017)
licence_note: Copyright NDSU. Read by R12 on 2026-11-16: unopened oil usually lasts about one to two years on the shelf depending on type; opened oil a few months to a year; refrigeration may extend storage life.

title: Food Storage: Will I Use It? (Live Well Utah newsletter, March)
licence_note: Copyright Utah State University. Read by R12 on 2026-11-16: shelf life halves for every 10.8 F rise (USDA, as quoted); best storage 40-60 F; dehydrated foods 10 percent or less moisture; with oxygen absorbers products must be dry (about 10 percent or less moisture) because botulism can occur in moist products in reduced-oxygen packaging; deep freeze (0 F) for 3 to 4 days kills pantry insects.

title: Jerky (drying recipe)
org: National Center for Home Food Preservation (University of Georgia)
licence_note: Copyright University of Georgia. Read by R12 on 2026-11-16: slice no thicker than 1/4 inch; keep meat at 40 F or below; internal temperature of 160 F necessary before drying (boil 5 minutes in marinade); alternative: heat dried strips 10 minutes in an oven preheated to 275 F; dehydrator preheated to 140 F; 10 to 24 hours if not preheated, check after 3 hours if heated in marinade; dry until a test piece cracks but does not break; two weeks at room temperature in a sealed container; refrigerate or freeze for longer.

title: Herbs (drying recipe)
org: National Center for Home Food Preservation (University of Georgia)
licence_note: Copyright University of Georgia. Read by R12 on 2026-11-16: dehydrator 95 to 115 F; up to 125 F in humid areas; dry when herbs crumble and stems break.

title: Drying Fruits (published August 1994, reviewed August 2025)
licence_note: Copyright Colorado State University. Read by R12 on 2026-11-16: dry at 140 F; condition loosely in containers two-thirds full in a warm, dry, ventilated place for 4 to 10 days, shaking daily; dry when squeezing leaves no moisture and pieces spring apart.

title: Storing Your Garden Harvest (August 2, 2019)
org: Washington State University Extension, Skagit County
licence_note: Copyright Washington State University. Read by R12 on 2026-11-16: cool and dry 50-60 F, 60-70% RH (pumpkins, winter squash); cold and dry 32-50 F, 60-70% (onions, garlic, dry beans); cold and moist 32-40 F, 80-90% (potatoes, apples, cabbage); cold and very moist 32-40 F, 90-95% (beets, carrots, parsnips, turnips and others); apples, pears and tomatoes produce ethylene; keep apples and pears away from cabbage, carrots, potatoes, onions.

title: Freezer Management
org: National Center for Home Food Preservation (University of Georgia)
licence_note: Copyright University of Georgia. Read by R12 on 2026-11-16: maintain the storage temperature at 0 F or lower; at higher temperatures foods lose quality much faster.

title: About Hantavirus (May 13, 2024)
licence_note: US federal government work, public domain. Read by R12 on 2026-11-16 through the web fetcher (curl from cdc.gov is refused): 38 percent of people who develop respiratory symptoms may die; symptoms usually 1 to 8 weeks after contact with an infected rodent; early fatigue, fever, muscle aches (thighs, hips, back); 4 to 10 days later coughing and shortness of breath; no specific treatment; deer mouse is the main US carrier.

title: How to Seal Up to Prevent Rodents (April 8, 2024)
licence_note: US federal government work, public domain. Read by R12 on 2026-11-16: mice can fit through a hole the width of a pencil (1/4 inch, 6 mm); steel wool with caulk or spray foam for small holes; lath screen or metal, cement, hardware cloth or metal sheeting for larger holes.

title: Controlling Stored-Food Insects (MF-2270, G. E. Lippert, January 1998)
org: Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station and Cooperative Extension Service
licence_note: Contents may be freely reproduced for educational purposes with credit (publication notice). Read by R12 on 2026-11-16: cold-treat at 0 F or lower for 3 days, larger packages 7 days; heat-treat flour, beans, nuts and whole grains in shallow pans in a 150 F oven for 15 to 20 minutes.

title: Selecting and Serving Produce Safely
licence_note: US federal government work, public domain. Read by R12 on 2026-11-16: children, older adults, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems should avoid eating raw or lightly cooked sprouts of any kind; cooking produce thoroughly kills harmful bacteria.
